turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the twenty-fifth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three headlines. Russia tells Estonia it is "on the verge" of open war — a week before Tallinn shuts its border.
[excited] Jensen Huang apologises to Nvidia's staff, for about an hour, and the Senate wants him on the third of December.
And Vietnam planned a four-day weekend for its first Culture Day. The factories cut it to a Tuesday.
[wry] So today's thread is — who keeps the calendar?

Dates someone else set. We start in Moscow. On Monday the twenty-third, Russia's foreign ministry summoned Estonia's chargé d'affaires, Marek Ühtegi, and told him Estonia's hostile steps were "on the verge of triggering open war".
[gasps] Open war. With a NATO member.
That's why it matters. Russia rarely uses the word war about a NATO member in an official statement.
NATO being the alliance where everyone promises to defend everyone else. So what set it off?

A border decision. On the twentieth, Estonia voted to shut its road crossings — Narva, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse — from the first of December, for at least six months. That followed an attempted arson attack on a drone maker, Threod Systems, near Tallinn, which Estonia blames on Russia's military intelligence.
And Moscow's complaint is about drones too.
It accuses Tallinn of letting Ukrainian drones cross its airspace "on the quiet" to strike Russia. And it "reserves the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures".
[skeptical] And Tallinn says?
Flat denial. The foreign ministry: "Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country."
And the defence minister, Kristo Herem, turned it right round — Russia is "definitely allowing Ukrainian drones to fly in its airspace more than they have flown in ours."
[deadpan] Delivered, one imagines, with some relish.
My favourite line on the page, though, is from a former defence official, Kaimo Kuusk, to ERR. "The bully is playing the victim." So how did the four capitals read it?
Moscow, via TASS. Maria Zakharova had already called a confirmed closure "yet another outburst of unbridled Russophobia".
Tallinn, via ERR — Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna calls the closure "a necessary step towards reducing security threats".
Kyiv's UA News read it as pressure after the Threod sabotage. And Al Jazeera, from Doha, quoted an Estonian lawmaker: "Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe."
And the sceptic?
The analyst Edmarverson Santos says the Russian statement names only political and diplomatic measures. Nothing military.
[curious] So "open war" is the headline, but the actual threat is… a strongly worded letter.
Roughly. And he turns on Tallinn as well. The Threod suspects came in through Latvia, per Interior Minister Igor Taro — so shutting the Russian road border wouldn't have stopped them.
And the cost lands on Narva.
The Russian-speaking border town. Its mayor, Jaan Toots, opposed the closure because families cross for "family events". One flag — the Taro remark is single-sourced.
Briefly, the Gulf. Iran says it hit tankers?

The Revolutionary Guards' navy said late on Monday that three oil tankers under American escort "suffered severe explosions and fires after striking naval mines" near Hormuz. [deadpan] It named no ships. No pictures. Footage, it said, would follow.
And Washington?
Central Command says every recognised primary lane is clear. It's the seventh such Iranian claim this month — about fifteen vessels, by one count.
Our sceptic box headline says it all. No ship, no mine, no picture.
A mine strike on a laden tanker leaves an insurance claim and a dry-dock booking. Until one surfaces, the desk prints the claim as a claim.
And the market barely moved. So — money. Oil, below ninety.
Brent settled at eighty-eight dollars thirty a barrel on Tuesday. Down from ninety-two fifty-seven on Friday, and its lowest since late August.
[excited] It closed above a hundred and seventeen on the thirtieth of October!

About a quarter gone. Traders cited signs of renewed talk between Washington and Tehran, President Trump saying he's in "no rush" to resume war with Iran, Gulf oil reaching buyers through bypass pipelines, and Libya restarting fields.
And why do we care, beyond the petrol pump?

Because oil is how this year's inflation got in. Two spikes, April and October, took American consumer prices from two point four per cent in February to three point seven by September. And the Fed has been raising rates against it.
So cheaper oil means the Fed can relax.
It weakens the case for the next rise. But the real yield — the cleanest measure of how tight money is — stayed at two point seven nine per cent.
And here's the calendar again. The Fed decides on the ninth of December.
November's inflation figures land on the tenth. [wry] A day after.
[laughs] Decide first, check the numbers second.
Which is where the Trend page comes in. Headline inflation jumped. But core — prices without food and fuel — never left a band of two point four five to two point eight two per cent all year.
So the oil shock went through prices… and out again?

That's the hope. Core was two point five seven in September. Hourly pay rose three point one two per cent, below inflation, so no wage spiral. And the bond market's implied ten-year inflation rate is at a one-year low, two point one three.
But there's a sceptic.

A Fed staff note from the ninth of November. Oil now leaks into core prices far more than it did — a lasting ten per cent rise lifts the core price level about seven times as much after three years as before the pandemic.
So this year's two spikes may still be working through. Okay — the Four, with their leans. And the usual line —

Explanation, not advice. V W R A: net asset value a hundred and seventy-eight dollars thirty-three on Monday, up three point one per cent on the Nvidia rally. Lean: lower into the ninth of December. Above a hundred and eighty-two on the second proves it wrong.
PIMCO Income?
The Singapore-dollar hedged class up nought point eight one per cent on the week, yielding six point eight six. Falling oil eases yields, which lifts bond prices. Lean: steady to firmer.
Gold and bitcoin?

Gold down two point three per cent, to three thousand five hundred and fifty-one dollars; with the real yield near two point eight, there's little to lift it. Bitcoin, fifty-nine thousand six hundred and thirty-nine, near the bottom of its one-year range. Both lean lower.
And the report card. Issue one sixty-six's leans came due today.
All four right. V W R A under its line, PIMCO better than its line, gold down with the real yield up, bitcoin under sixty-four thousand four hundred.
[laughs] Four for four. Take a bow.
[deadpan] I'll bow when the next four land. Still not advice.
Home desk. Lawrence Wong was in Canberra yesterday —

— for the eleventh Annual Leaders' Meeting with Anthony Albanese. Two documents signed. A treaty letting Singapore ship captured carbon dioxide to Australia to store under the seabed — we have nowhere to bury our own. And a wider emergency-supplies pact: ten categories, including food, semiconductors, medicines and fertiliser.
And the dependence runs both ways, doesn't it?

Singapore's refineries supply fifty-five per cent of Australia's petrol, on Canberra's own July figures. Mr Wong: "These are practical arrangements that will make a real difference when the next disruption comes."
Sceptic?

Louise Morris of the Australia Institute. The treaty text "is not public", Canberra must indemnify past operators "indefinitely, with no cap and no sunset clause", and Chevron's Gorgon project "missed its targets by about fifty per cent".
[wry] Australians, she says, left "holding the bill". Right. Technology.
Jensen Huang's first all-hands since the board took him back. Santa Clara, Tuesday. He apologised for about an hour.
[sighs] "I made some terrible mistakes," he said, according to reports of the livestream. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and of course, I hurt all of you." He said he's in therapy.

And Washington wants its turn. Senate Banking chairman Tim Scott has called a hearing on export controls for the third of December, with Huang as a witness. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is invited for the tenth.
And the governance changed with him?
CNBC reports Harvey Jones as newly appointed chair. The Wall Street Journal, via AFP, says Huang's direct reports will now send reviews of his behaviour to the board. [wry] Imagine writing that one.
And the shares?
Gave back five point eight per cent on Tuesday, to a hundred and fifty-five dollars forty-nine — a day after a thirty-one and a half per cent jump.
The sceptic is a former SK hynix researcher, Lee Joo-wan. On the bills behind the hearing: "Workarounds will always emerge."

He expects Beijing to push harder for its own chips, which shrinks Washington's leverage rather than growing it. One more flag: the Attorney General told Fox there was "no evidence" of crimes. A single-outlet report.
Home Lab! Ant Group has put out Ling three point two air.

A free model under the M I T licence, so a company can fold it into a product and sell it without asking. A hundred and twenty-four billion parameters — but only five and a half billion wake up for each word.
[curious] How does that work?
It's a mixture of experts: five hundred and twelve specialist sub-networks, and eight fire at a time. So a big model runs at the speed of a small one.
And it fits on what?
A compressed copy needs about eighty gigabytes. So a Mac Studio, or a mini PC, with a hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes of shared memory.
Is it any good?
Artificial Analysis gives it twenty-three on its Intelligence Index, among the leaders in its open class, where the median is five. But it's wordy. And there's no independent speed figure yet.
The sceptic's quote is great. Elias Hawthorne of OrcaRouter: "At sixty-one per cent, two of every five workflows still fail."
[wry] He also sells routing between models. The page notes it.
The Kit. vivo's V eighty, in Singapore at eight hundred and ninety-nine Singapore dollars.
Pre-orders to the twenty-sixth, shops from Friday. The usual price is nine hundred and ninety-nine; the hundred-dollar cut ends on the thirty-first of December.
And the hook is — the Apple Watch.
The first Android phone vivo says can take an Apple Watch's notifications and health data.
[excited] The thing everyone leaving an iPhone asks!
The catch, per GSMArena: the watch must first be paired with an iPhone.
[laughs] Of course it must.

A seven thousand two hundred milliamp-hour battery, a three-times ZEISS zoom, and an I P sixty-nine rating against hot high-pressure jets. Skip it if you want wireless charging, fast cable transfers — it's U S B two — or the newest chip.
The Atelier. Candles. And I learned the soot isn't really the wax's fault.
Look at the wick. A Danish Environmental Protection Agency study found that for some candles "virtually the entire emitted particle mass" was the salts in the wick. Not soot.
And the "natural" waxes?

Refined paraffin won. A paraffin pillar gave off about a hundred and four thousand ultrafine particles per cubic centimetre; an animal-stearin candle up to four hundred and thirty thousand. Though candle makers co-funded the study.
[chuckles] So what am I paying for in a fancy candle?

The glass. Soy wax is about four pounds thirty a kilo in bulk, so the wax in a sixty-three-pound Diptyque is worth roughly one pound. Best tip on the page: trim the wick to five millimetres. It does more than the label.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single morning.
Juggling!
Juggling. And it starts with a man on roller skates.
David Rush, the Idaho record-hunter. On the twenty-third, Guinness confirmed he skated thirty-one thousand eight hundred and sixteen metres along the Boise Greenbelt —
— while juggling three balls. A run he made in October twenty twenty-five. More than six times the old mark.
[laughs] And his quote: "When you're juggling and skating, a pebble the size of a pea can lock up a wheel."
Spoken like a man who has met that pebble.
Okay, basics. Juggling is keeping more objects in the air than you have hands. The gateway is the cascade — three balls, each crossing hand to hand in a figure of eight.
Most people never get past three balls. And most people could.
Loh Koah Fong, who brought organised juggling to Singapore in the nineteen-nineties, promises a beginner —
"I bet you can do a simple three-ball cascade within two weeks!"
[excited] With an exclamation mark, in the original. And then, Claire — the mathematics. Claude Shannon.
The founder of information theory. He built the first juggling robot, and wrote a theorem relating time in the air, time in the hand, balls and hands.
And Ron Graham — a giant of combinatorics — was president of the International Jugglers' Association in nineteen seventy-two.
[deadpan] The mathematicians were juggling the whole time. Explains a great deal.
Then, the nineteen-eighties. Three groups — Santa Cruz, Caltech and Cambridge — independently invent siteswap.
A notation. Any pattern written as a string of numbers, each the height of a throw counted in beats. "Three" is the cascade. "Four four one" is a three-ball pattern called the half-box.
[curious] Wait — four, four, one. Why is that three balls?
Here's the rule that makes it a game. The number of balls is the average of the throws. Four plus four plus one is nine, over three throws. Three.
[laughs] Oh, that's lovely.
And a string that doesn't average to a whole number can't be juggled. So a computer can list every pattern that can.
Which is what Jack Boyce did. He wrote most of the free Juggling Lab animator, and found the longest "prime" siteswaps in nineteen ninety-nine.
More vocabulary. A shower is five one. Mills Mess crosses the arms — but it's still siteswap three.
And Rubenstein's Revenge is five two two three three.
[deadpan] Which sounds like a lottery ticket.
And the world behind it is bigger than it looks. The European Juggling Convention drew six thousand five hundred and seventy-three people to Arnhem in twenty twenty-five.

Up from two thousand three hundred and eleven in Lublin two years earlier. At the very top, Alex Barron of London was the first to flash fourteen balls — throw and catch each one once — in twenty seventeen.
Fourteen. [gasps] I can barely flash two. Gear, then — beanbags first, because they land dead.
NetJuggler, the French shop, tells beginners exactly that: "they don't roll on the ground when they fall!"
And clubs are a German speciality. Henrys of Karlsruhe has a new carbon Numbers Club — "only a hundred and sixty grams" — at fifty-four pounds ninety-nine.
Then the deep end. Flowtoys' Vision L E D clubs, about five hundred and ninety US dollars for three. And the passing kit's listing reads: "pass juggling partner and friend not included".
[laughs] Brutal. And Singapore? Do we have a shop?
No juggling shop. The last specialist, Jugglenaut, closed in two thousand, by one account. But the Bishan Community Club runs a free circus-arts interest group for juggling and yo-yo.
And the ninety-day plan?

Weeks one to three: three Play beanbags, about twenty pounds, plus the free Juggling Lab, and the cascade. By week eight, Henrys Delphin clubs and a free club night at Bishan. By week thirteen, five balls. Buy-once total: two hundred and fifty to three hundred and fifty pounds, before shipping and G S T.
And now the brain claim. Because that's why a lot of adults start.
In two thousand and four, Bogdan Draganski and colleagues reported in Nature that grey matter grew in twelve volunteers learning the cascade. And shrank back when they stopped.

An Oxford team found white-matter change after six weeks. But its lead, Heidi Johansen-Berg, said MRI is "an indirect way to measure brain structure and so we cannot be sure exactly what is changing."
And the Hamburg authors themselves: further training "does not seem to alter brain structure." Gains that vanish when practice stops are learning, not a lasting upgrade. Juggle for the pleasure.
[warmly] And Jesse Shavel's rule for the plateau, in the I J A's eJuggle: "If it doesn't feel easy, take a step back."
Good advice for most of this programme.
Culture and the body. Thanksgiving at the cinema — Hexed against the Fockers.

Disney Animation's Hexed and Universal's Focker-In-Law open in America today. Deadline tracks each at about forty to fifty million US dollars over five days. Critics split them: on Rotten Tomatoes, Hexed sixty-five per cent, Focker-In-Law twenty-nine.
[chuckles] Though Glenn Kenny at RogerEbert dot com admitted the Fockers made him laugh. "Readers, I did."
The sceptic: Box Office Theory puts Hexed at only about twenty-three million — which, on a reported budget of a hundred and fifty million, would be a flop. Hexed opens here tomorrow, by one listing.
The Good Life. A thirty-one-year-old Parisian named Théo Auffret.
[amused] Good name.
[laughs] Excellent name. His titanium tourbillon sold at Phillips in Hong Kong for twelve point one nine million Hong Kong dollars. Nearly seven times its high estimate.

A tourbillon is a rotating cage that carries a watch's regulating parts round once a minute, to average out gravity. The read: the premium has moved from the name on the dial to the person at the bench.
And the sceptic?
SJX's own preview: he built the run with "more scalable methods" — computer-milled parts, outsourced cases. So the price pays for scarcity and the Journe prize, not hours at the bench.
Family Desk. The Kpod rules.
The ministries' figures: three hundred and sixty-seven of the one thousand five hundred and forty-four people caught with etomidate vapes were caught again. About one in five.
And under-sixteens who reoffend now do a twenty-four-week intensive programme at the Institute of Mental Health.
The line a parent needs: "Those who voluntarily seek help will not face any penalties or have an offence record."
[warmly] And the sceptic's advice is lovely. Two hundred and thirty-eight student referrals in a quarter is a real problem, and a small share of children. Talk; don't search bags.
General guidance, not legal or medical advice.
Fitness. A review in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, by Glenn Gaesser and Robert Sallis, ranks movement over diet.
The poorest diets carried three to twenty per cent higher mortality. Sitting most of the day, forty-six to more than a hundred and sixty-three per cent.
And a sedentary person adding two thousand steps a day — about one point six kilometres — was tied to twenty-five to fifty per cent lower risk.
Sallis: "Exercise is the more powerful medication, but you should do both together."
[skeptical] But then — the Finnish twins.

Laura Joensuu followed twenty-two thousand seven hundred and fifty Finnish twins for up to forty-five years. Going from sedentary to moderately active cut mortality by only seven per cent, with no gain beyond.
So genes explain much of the link. And the review itself is narrative, not a formal meta-analysis.
General guidance, not medical advice. The cheapest gains sit at the bottom of the ladder — which is also where the twins found their only effect.
And a Diary pick?
Maruyama Ôkyo at the Edo-Tokyo Museum. Advance tickets close at eleven fifty-nine on Friday night, Japan time. Under-eighteens go free, so only adults need to buy.
And for the kids at home — Horrible Histories at the Drama Centre, twenty-ninth to thirty-first of January. No refunds, mind.
The Undercurrent. [pause] Yesterday, Vietnam stopped work for its first Culture Day.
[thoughtful] Its first new paid public holiday in seven years.
The date is old. On the twenty-fourth of November, nineteen forty-six, Ho Chi Minh spoke at the Hanoi Opera House, and left a line every Vietnamese schoolchild knows.
"Culture lights the way for the nation."
Eighty years on, the state made it a day off. With an economic purpose. The Party wants cultural industries at seven per cent of output by twenty thirty, against roughly four to five now.
So a day off is meant to create the customers.
In early September, the Ministry of Home Affairs proposed a four-day break, Saturday to Tuesday. To "boost consumer spending". The union backed it.
And then?
[pause] Ten days later, the plan was gone. Late November is when companies "speed up production, fill orders and meet annual targets."
[sighs] The order book.
So the first Culture Day was a lone Tuesday, in the middle of the export season.

[warmly] And firms rebuilt the weekend themselves, where they could. Ho Tay International gave its two thousand two hundred workers four days. A garment firm in Ho Chi Minh City gave its fifty-odd workers four days. A printer gave one, with Saturday shifts and extra overtime.
And Nguyen Thi Hoa, a garment worker, planned to take her children home to Vinh Long… to see their grandparents.
[thoughtful] That's the bit that stays with me.
South Korea is the hinge. It demoted Hangul Day to a working commemoration in nineteen ninety to ninety-one, for a factory economy. And restored it in twenty twelve.
The industrial state cut its culture holiday. The culture-exporting state brought it back.
And the desk's call: in twenty twenty-seven, Culture Day falls on a Wednesday. It will be a single day, with no bridging swap.
The sceptic says it's just the calendar — it fell on a Tuesday, and Tết and National Day already carry the long breaks.
Fair. But the four-day plan was the state's own, written for consumption. It was the production calendar that killed it.
[pause] Vietnam can legislate the day off. It cannot yet legislate the leisure economy the day off is meant to feed.
The show at My Dinh Stadium ran on Tuesday night all the same. People will look forward to every twenty-fourth of November…
[warmly] If the factories let them.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-five pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
